items.headline: What work can robots do?
items.author: Russell Legate-Yang and Maxim Massenkoff
items.caption: Key findings (full section): 74%/34%, 80%, 0.3%/40 years, 50-year backtest, 2%/year

highlights.label: three-quarters of physical tasks / 34% of working hours
highlights.text: Robots, which we define as autonomous physical machines that sense and act, can perform three-quarters of physical tasks in the US, making up 34% of working hours, but mostly in limited settings.

highlights.label: workers exposed are male, less educated, lower paid
highlights.text: Workers exposed to robots are more likely to be male, less educated, and lower paid.

highlights.label: about 80% exposed to robots or LLMs
highlights.text: Overall, about 80% of job tasks by working time are exposed to either robots or LLMs.

highlights.label: much more expensive than human labor
highlights.text: While robots can do most physical work tasks today, they are much more expensive than human labor.

highlights.label: cost-competitive for just 0.3%
highlights.text: Robots are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of job tasks.

highlights.label: 40 years to reach 10%
highlights.text: If robot price declines follow past trends, it will take 40 years for that share to reach 10%.

highlights.label: past 50 years: greater declines in wages and employment
highlights.text: Over the past 50 years, jobs more exposed to robots experienced greater declines in wages and employment than others.

highlights.label: 2% of previously impossible physical work per year
highlights.text: each year, robots have become able to do about 2% of the physical work they previously couldn’t.

items.slide_topic: work: robots + LLMs expose all but one-fifth
items.headline: What work can robots do?
items.author: Russell Legate-Yang and Maxim Massenkoff
items.caption: Introduction paragraphs: 74% of physical tasks = 34% of working hours; robots and LLMs expose all but one-fifth of employment; cost-competitive for just 0.3%

highlights.label: 74% of physical tasks = 34% of working hours
highlights.text: We find that robots can already perform 74% of physical tasks in the US, making up 34% of working hours.

highlights.label: robots + LLMs expose all but one-fifth
highlights.text: Robots and LLMs together expose all but one-fifth of employment.

highlights.label: cost-competitive for just 0.3% of work
highlights.text: But we also find significant barriers to adoption: most robots require highly structured environments, and are cost-competitive with people for just 0.3% of work.

highlights.label: 40 years to reach just 10%
highlights.text: If robot price declines follow past trends, it will take 40 years for that share to reach just 10%.

items.headline: What work can robots do?
items.author: Russell Legate-Yang and Maxim Massenkoff
items.caption: Cost-adoption scenarios paragraph: 50% of physical work cost-competitive by 2085 (3%/yr) vs 2050 (fast); 90% still takes 53 years

highlights.label: half of physical work cost-competitive only by 2085 (3%/yr)
highlights.text: Adding in 3% cost declines per year, robots aren’t cost-competitive for half of physical work today until 2085.

highlights.label: fast scenario: half of physical work by 2050
highlights.text: In a fast adoption scenario, where quality-adjusted costs fall up to four times faster and robots become able to do new tasks twice as fast, robots become cost-competitive for half of physical work by 2050.

highlights.label: 90% of physical work still takes 53 years
highlights.text: Automating 90% of physical work today still takes 53 years.

items.headline: The machines have a type: male, blue-collar and lower-paid
items.dek: A new Anthropic study finds the jobs most exposed to physical automation are held mostly by men, with fewer qualifications and smaller pay packets. But the price tag means no stampede is imminent.

items.slide_topic: work: how Claude rated each task (data release)
items.headline: Task: Drive taxicabs or privately owned vehicles to transport passengers. (Taxi Drivers, O*NET task 23762) - rated E3
items.dek: All instances occur on public roads and curbs, an unstructured setting, so the cap is E3 throughout. Waymo's commercial driverless service (≈3,500 vehicles, ~500k paid rides/week, 220M+ rider-only miles, freeway and airport curbside service, 24/7 availability), corroborated by Zoox in Las Vegas, supports E3 for instances 0 (urban core, 30), 1 (suburban, 20), 2 (airport/freeway, 15) and 3 (late night, 15) = 80 weight. Instances 4 (snow/ice/flood, 10) and 5 (wheelchair/assisted mobility, 10) are E0: winter and floodwater operations are explicitly paused, and WAV rides remain human-driven with no automated securement. Qualifying weight: E1 = 80, E2 = 80, E3 = 80 — all above 50, so the task tier is E3.
items.author: Claude Opus 5 with web search (per data README)
items.caption: Claude's own written reasoning for the taxi-driver task rating (E3), verbatim from the data release; cited sources include Waymo, electrek.co, waymo.com/safety/impact
items.notes: Verbatim `reasoning` field. These are Claude's rating justifications with figures Claude cited from web sources (Waymo ~3,500 vehicles, ~500k paid rides/week, 220M+ rider-only miles) - not independently verified by us. time_share=0.4118. Good for a d.terminal() card.

items.slide_topic: work: how Claude rated each task (data release)
items.headline: Task: Weld components in flat, vertical, or overhead positions. (Welders, Cutters, Solderers, and Brazers, O*NET task 23582) - rated E1
items.dek: E1 qualifying weight = 100 (every instance: Path Robotics scanning cells for shop and one-off fabrication, Novarc SWR for pipe spools, RAMLAB MaxQ cells for wear-part rebuild, plus the field instances, which arise unproblematically once the work is fixtured in a cell). E2 qualifying weight = 40 (instance 1, heavy/structural and ship-block welding, 25, on HD Hyundai's self-driving collaborative welding robots working inside blocks on the plant floor; plus instance 3, field standardized joints, 15) — short of a majority, because production bench welding (25), pipe spool welding (15), one-off field work (10) and wear-part repair (10) are substantiated only at a purpose-built station or cell. E3 qualifying weight = 15 (Shimizu Robo-Welder column splices on a live construction site). Decisive: instances 0, 2, 4 and 5 cap at E1, so the highest tier with >50 weight is E1.
items.author: Claude Opus 5 with web search (per data README)
items.caption: Claude's reasoning for the welding task rating (E1); cites Path Robotics AW-3 cells, Novarc SWR, HD Hyundai, Shimizu Robo-Welder
items.notes: Verbatim `reasoning` field from the data release. Article body quotes the Path Robotics sentence for this same task (footnote 21).

datasets.title: Annual cost of robots vs median human compensation, five physical occupations
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?", Figure 7 (BLS OEWS 2025, ECEC 2026; costs estimated by Claude)
datasets.notes: Robot cost is for performing the exposed tasks only (e.g. 97% of packers' time), so compare to compensation x exposed share: packers 47.5 vs 45.4 (robots cheaper), taxi 50.5 vs 57.8 (robots $7K dearer - text: "around $7,000 more"), welders ~5x human cost. Text rounds packers' robot cost to ~$45,000 vs ~$49,000 pay, "about $2,500 less per year".

datasets.title: How far robot costs must fall before robots undercut humans (selected occupations)
datasets.source: DERIVED from Anthropic Fig. 7 numbers: 1 - (median comp x exposed share) / annual robot cost; Postal Service value (54%) is stated in the Figure 8 caption
datasets.notes: My calculation (not printed in the article): packers 0 (already cost-competitive), taxi 1-(56.8*0.89)/57.8=12.5%, dishwashers 1-45/172=73.8%, welders 1-(73.4*0.9)/334.6=80.3%, janitors 1-(47.7*0.73)/280=87.6%. These match the marker positions on Figure 8 (taxi ~12%, dishwashers ~74%, welders ~80%, janitors ~88%) to within ~1 point. Label as "derived".

datasets.title: LLM exposure vs LLM-and-robot exposure by occupation group (DIGITIZED from the radar chart, +-1 pp)
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?", Figure 6 - values measured by me from dot positions in the 7680 px original image; NOT published numerically by Anthropic
datasets.notes: Method: located the 44 dots (blue/orange) by colour, fitted the radar centre from spoke geometry (rms 0.06 px at 1600 px scale) and scaled radius to 100%. Calibration is validated by the caption (Protective service 31% and 61% -> measured 31.0 and 61.0) and by text (Transportation & moving "<15%" -> "about 90%": measured 13.1 -> 90.7; Office & admin "nearly 100%": 98.2; Personal care & service "around 40%": 41.8; "no occupation group is less than 40% exposed": min 41.8). For Business & financial, Community & social service and Legal the orange dot is hidden behind the blue one (difference <1.5 pp; Legal set equal). Treat as approximate on slides ("~").

datasets.notes: Approximate inputs: overall LLM-only is "around half"; transportation LLM-only is "less than 15%" (upper bound, digitized value 13); both robot values are exact (81, 61) or "about 90". datasets.title: US job tasks by robot exposure over time (robots as of each year)
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix Figure 4 (p. 11 of appendix PDF); Census/ACS employment weights
datasets.notes: Only the labelled values are given; unlabeled slices are null (1991: E2+E3 = 2; 2002: E2+E3 = 3; 2008 E3 ~0 by sum). The 2026 bar is Census/ACS-weighted (physical = 40%), whereas main Figure 3 is OEWS-weighted (physical = 46%). Text: physical work fell from 53% of tasks to 40% (-13 pp, a 25% decline).

datasets.title: Barriers to robot automation of physical tasks (today)
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix Figure 10 (p. 25) and Appendix C.2
datasets.notes: Tasks can have multiple barriers, so shares exceed 100%. Main text: capabilities "around 70%", manipulation "half", planning & reasoning 8%, regulation 14%, preferences "a quarter". Appendix: only 26% of physical tasks cannot be done by robots in any environment; "only about 30% of tasks are limited by either preferences or regulation".

datasets.title: Backtest: effect of historical robot exposure on wages and employment over ~20 years
datasets.unit: change vs unexposed occupation in same industry, per fully exposed occupation
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix Figure 5 and B.3
datasets.notes: Text: a fully robot-exposed occupation had wages 7.1% lower (95% CI 5.4% to 8.9%) and lost 34.2% of its jobs (95% CI 16.4% to 52.0%) over about 20 years relative to an unexposed occupation in the same industry. Pooled 3 periods 1977-2024; placebo: 1977 exposure has no effect on 1970-1980 wages.

datasets.title: Robot adoption scenarios: year robots become cost-competitive
datasets.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" main text (2085 / 2050) and Appendix E / Appendix Figure 12 (janitors 2095; rapid: "2050s")
datasets.notes: Other stated timeline points: business as usual - robots cost-competitive for 10% of human work "until the 2060s"; ~40 years at 3%/yr; by 2075 robots can do 90% of physical tasks in the "broadening" variant. Rapid advances (12%/yr hardware, 6%/yr other costs) - 10% of work time by "around 2040", robot janitors in the 2050s; automating 90% of today's physical work still takes 53 years. By 2040 business-as-usual projects robots cost-competitive for 2.5 million jobs in occupations where robots can do at least 85% of tasks (600,000 to 3 million across the 95% and 75% thresholds) - the authors call 2.5 million "more of a ceiling on job loss than a central estimate"; the China trade shock cost an estimated 2-2.4 million jobs over 1999-2011.

facts.claim: Anthropic economists: robots can already perform 74% of physical tasks in the US - 34% of all working hours - but mostly in controlled settings.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: About 80% of job tasks by working time are exposed to robots or LLMs; LLMs alone expose about half of work, robots + LLMs 81%.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Robots are cost-competitive for just 0.3% of job tasks; at past price trends (about 3% a year) it takes 40 years to reach 10%.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Of all US work: 54% cognitive/interpersonal, 12% no robot can do (E0), 23% robots can do in purpose-built environments (E1), 10% in structured human workplaces (E2), 1% in unstructured environments (E3).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Of physical tasks: 26.3% E0, 49.8% E1, 22.0% E2, only 1.9% E3 (unstructured settings such as roads).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: 9 of the 10 most robot-exposed occupations are vehicle operators; taxi drivers lead with an index of 2.2 (scale 0-3), citing Waymo robotaxis.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Robots broaden AI exposure to the physical economy: transportation & moving tasks exposed to LLMs alone <15% but ~90% with robots; office & admin to nearly 100%; protective service 31% -> 61%; personal care ~40%; no occupation group is less than 40% exposed.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Most robot-exposed workers are male, less educated, lower paid: 20 pp less likely to be female, 55 pp less likely to have a bachelor's degree, ~$30/hour lower wages ($22.88 vs $52.97), unemployment 5.2% vs 2.2% (top quintile vs unexposed).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Barriers beyond cost: capabilities block ~70% of physical tasks (manipulation ~half), human preferences ~a quarter, regulation 14%; cost is a barrier for nearly every task (97%).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Packers and packagers (560,000 US jobs) are the largest occupation where robots are already cost-competitive: robots costing >$2 million replace ~14 workers; ~$45,000 a year vs ~$49,000 pay; employment already down 22% since 2015.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Robotaxis cost only around $7,000 a year more than taxi drivers but face regulatory hurdles; robot welders cost ~5x human welders, robot janitors $280,000 a year vs $47,700 pay.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: If robots cost 20% less, they would be cost-competitive for the physical work of 2.8 million workers (0.8% of all working time); a 70% price drop is needed for 10% of human work.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Robots have gained about 2% a year on previously impossible physical work: in 1977 robots could not do 62% of physical tasks; today all but 24%.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: Standard scenario (3%/yr robot cost declines): robots not cost-competitive for half of physical work until 2085; fast scenario (costs fall up to 4x faster, capabilities 2x faster): by 2050; automating 90% of physical work still takes 53 years.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: 50-year backtest: occupations with all tasks robot-exposed saw wages 7.1% lower (95% CI 5.4-8.9) and employment 34.2% lower (CI 16.4-52.0) over ~20 years than unexposed ones in the same industry.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix B.3

facts.claim: Method: ~900 O*NET occupations / ~19,000 tasks; 7,594 physical tasks rated E0-E3 by Claude with web search, citing real robots; Claude made ~650,000 web searches and cited over 275,000 quotes from 90,000+ pages (incl. historical ratings).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix A.3

facts.claim: The data release states the ratings were produced by Claude Opus 5 (with web search) on O*NET 29.3 tasks; data are CC BY 4.0 (923 occupations, 18,796 tasks).
facts.source: Anthropic data release README (Hugging Face)

facts.claim: Robustness caveat: excluding ratings that rely on robots doing only related tasks lowers the exposed share of physical work from about three-quarters to about a half; dropping demonstration-only evidence lowers it by 1 point.
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix A.4

facts.claim: Of 923 O*NET occupations in the data release, 264 have robot exposure index 0.0 (unweighted mean 0.395); e.g. Registered Nurses 0.014, Software Developers 0.0, Electricians 0.33, Plumbers 0.51, Taxi Drivers 2.22.
facts.source: Anthropic data release, robot_exposure_occupations.csv (counted/aggregated by me)

facts.claim: Spending on robots is about 1% of US equipment investment; surveys suggest US robot adoption could nearly double within three years (13% of firms use robotics now, 22% expect to).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" (Legate-Yang & Massenkoff)

facts.claim: By 2040 under business-as-usual, robots become cost-competitive for 2.5 million jobs in occupations where robots can do at least 85% of tasks (0.6-3 million at 95%/75% thresholds); the authors call this "more of a ceiling on job loss than a central estimate" (China trade shock: 2-2.4 million jobs).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix E

facts.claim: Physical tasks fell from 53% of US job tasks in 1977 to 40% today (Census-weighted; 46% in the OEWS-weighted Figure 3).
facts.source: Anthropic, "What work can robots do?" Appendix B.2

facts.claim: Press: CNBC-TV18 (Oct 2, 2026): "The machines have a type: male, blue-collar and lower-paid" - "...the price tag means no stampede is imminent."
facts.source: CNBC-TV18 (Asmi Saxena)
